UPDATE 1-Activision shareholders reach $250 million settlement over Microsoft buyout
Shareholders in the maker of the "Call of Duty" video game, led by Swedish pension fund Sjunde AP-Fonden, accused former Activision Blizzard executives including Chief Executive Bobby Kotick of breaching their fiduciary duties to investors by agreeing to a $95 per share takeover price. The shareholders said Kotick rushed into the merger so he could keep his job and $400 million of change-of-control benefits.
Shareholders of Activision Blizzard reached a $250 million settlement over allegations that the company's former executives and Microsoft shortchanged them when Microsoft acquired the game maker for $75.4 billion in 2023, according to a late Thursday court filing in a Delaware state court. Shareholders in the maker of the "Call of Duty" video game, led by Swedish pension fund Sjunde AP-Fonden, accused former Activision Blizzard executives including Chief Executive Bobby Kotick of breaching their fiduciary duties to investors by agreeing to a $95 per share takeover price.
The shareholders said Kotick rushed into the merger so he could keep his job and $400 million of change-of-control benefits. Microsoft and Kotick brought counterclaims against Sjunde, which will also be resolved in the settlement agreement.

sources.news_title: Activision shareholders reach $250 million settlement over Microsoft buyout
Microsoft, Activision Blizzard Shareholders Reach $250M Settlement
Microsoft pays $250 million to end lawsuit over Activision Blizzard buyout
sources.text:
Activision Blizzard shareholders just landed a $250 million payout from Microsoft, and the story behind how they got it is something else.
The saga started in 2022, when the gaming giant’s stock had cratered amid a wave of sexual harassment and misconduct allegations. Rather than waiting for the storm to pass, Activision’s then-CEO Bobby Kotick negotiated a sale to Microsoft, agreeing to an acquisition price that a Swedish pension fund called embarrassingly low.
The fund argued shareholders got shortchanged because the company was undervalued at the time of the deal. That argument, it turned out, was worth a quarter of a billion dollars.
Microsoft agrees to pay $250 million to settle Activision shareholder lawsuit
As reported by Bloomberg Law, Microsoft agreed Friday to pay $250 million to end shareholder litigation over its $75.4 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard, according to court filings. The settlement was reached in Delaware’s Chancery Court, where the case had been grinding along for three years.
The lawsuit was brought by AP7, a Swedish pension fund that manages retirement savings for millions of Swedish workers. AP7’s central claim was that Kotick, who served as Activision’s CEO during the scandal and the acquisition, rushed the Microsoft deal to protect himself from the fallout. By selling while the company’s share price was depressed, AP7 argued, Activision’s board locked shareholders into a sale price that was far lower than it should have been.
A judge let the case move forward against Kotick and other board members last October, though she rejected allegations that Microsoft had colluded with them to drive down the deal price. With Microsoft now settling, neither party has admitted wrongdoing.
The case grew stranger as it went. Kotick, represented by high-profile attorney Alex Spiro, filed a counterclaim alleging the lawsuit was not what it appeared.
He claimed AP7’s vice chairman had previously worked at Embracer Group, a rival gaming company, and accused the fund of filing the suit on Embracer’s behalf to hobble Activision competitively. Embracer flatly denied any coordination. AP7 dismissed the entire theory as revisionist history that was both legally and factually frivolous.
Related
The Activision acquisition was one of the most scrutinized deals in gaming history, drawing opposition from regulators in the US, UK, and Europe before finally closing in 2023.
The $250 million will go to Activision shareholders who were affected by the deal. Court approval is still required before any money changes hands.
For more on how Microsoft’s acquisition of Activision reshaped the gaming industry, and the enormous payday Bobby Kotick walked away with when the deal closed, we have you covered.
